action_summary: Asks whether the repertoire is a possession or a query, on the real machine, with zero model calls. The machine's shell catalogue is read program by program (uncapped discovery, deduped by real path): 437 programs, 492 pages, 13,250 option lines, 4,621 distinct options, 1,147,792 bytes, in 46.6 s and nothing stored. Then 164 sampled options are EXECUTED against a real state (a real repo, archive, gzip, patch) with an object bound from the state whenever the program itself asks for one: 80 are accepted by their own program and 0 change a byte. An option is a modifier, not an action: the page never says which program is a mutator and never binds the object. Second negative: for 12 real needs written before the run, the catalogue's own words give top-3 page scores of 7.55 when a shell can serve the need and 5.36 when nothing can, with no threshold separating them; the top answer for undoing a merge was `lzfgrep`. Also a defect in our own organ: discover_v1.binaries() truncates at 400 names ALPHABETICALLY, so `git` was invisible to the project's discovery until this round asked for the uncapped list. 4 of 8 declared criteria met, 1 failed, 2 void and reported as void. 0 parameters, 0 model calls, no network at run time.

truth.the_law_this_round_adds: THE VERBS ARE FREE, THE PURPOSE IS NOT. A machine will tell you what it can be asked to do (437 programs, 4,621 options, 46.6 s, 0 parameters) and will not tell you what to do, to what, or why: 0 of 80 accepted options changed a state, and 12 needs were indistinguishable from the ones the machine cannot serve. Stored repertoires are therefore both unnecessary (the query is cheap and cannot go stale) and insufficient (the catalogue has no purpose in it).
